meta.title: How a Poem Gets Its Echo
meta.skill_frame: Author's craft: read how the writer explains the choices that built a poem.

reader.who: Students who read at about a twelfth-grade level.
reader.why_this_level: Verbatim, measured FK 14.8/13.1/25.6 over the three parts (247, 213, and 222 words). The load is an abstract first-person account of composition: long periodic sentences, a chain of choices, and assumed knowledge of poetry terms.
reader.tone: Adult subject. Plain sentences. The lesson must not make the reader feel small.

source.basis: Verbatim from Edgar Allan Poe, "The Philosophy of Composition" (1846), public domain.
source.attribution: Poe, Edgar Allan. "The Philosophy of Composition." 1846. Project Gutenberg eBook #55749, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/55749, accessed 2026-11-11. Public domain in the United States.
source.survey: A writer explains the choices that produced a poem, from length and tone to the refrain and its single word.
source.avoided: No invented detail; the passage is Poe's text as published.

session.difficulty_basis: an abstract first-person account of composition with long periodic sentences and assumed poetry terms

authoring_exceptions: Parts run 213-247 words; verbatim grade-12 prose split only at sentence boundaries.

script_overrides.near_copy_2: Say it in your own words. One sentence is enough.

passage.part_1: Melancholy is thus the most legitimate of all the poetical tones. The length, the province, and the tone, being thus determined, I betook myself to ordinary induction, with the view of obtaining some artistic piquancy which might serve me as a keynote in the construction of the poem—some pivot upon which the whole structure might turn. In carefully thinking over all the usual artistic effects—or more properly points, in the theatrical sense—I did not fail to perceive immediately that no one had been so universally employed as that of the refrain. The universality of its employment sufficed to assure me of its intrinsic value, and spared me the necessity of submitting it to analysis. I considered it, however, with regard to its susceptibility of improvement, and soon saw it to be in a primitive condition. As commonly used, the refrain, or burden, not only is limited to lyric verse, but depends for its impression upon the force of monotone—both in sound and thought. The pleasure is deduced solely from the sense of identity—of repetition. I resolved to diversify, and so heighten, the effect, by adhering, in general, to the monotone of sound, while I continually varied that of thought: that is to say, I determined to produce continuously novel effects, by the variation of the application of the refrain—the refrain itself remaining, for the most part, unvaried. These points being settled, I next bethought me of the nature of my refrain.
passage.part_2: Since its application was to be repeatedly varied, it was clear that the refrain itself must be brief, for there would have been an insurmountable difficulty in frequent variations of application in any sentence of length. In proportion to the brevity of the sentence, would, of course, be the facility of the variation. This led me at once to a single word as the best refrain. The question now arose as to the character of the word. Having made up my mind to a refrain, the division of the poem into stanzas was, of course, a corollary, the refrain forming the close of each stanza. That such a close, to have force, must be sonorous and susceptible of protracted emphasis, admitted no doubt; and these considerations inevitably led me to the long “o” as the most sonorous vowel, in connection with “r” as the most producible consonant. The sound of the refrain being thus determined, it became necessary to select a word embodying this sound, and at the same time in the fullest possible keeping with that melancholy which I had predetermined as the tone of the poem. In such a search it would have been absolutely impossible to overlook the word “Nevermore.” In fact, it was the very first which presented itself.
passage.part_3: The next desideratum was a pretext for the continuous use of the one word “Nevermore.” In observing the difficulty which I at once found in inventing a sufficiently plausible reason for its continuous repetition, I did not fail to perceive that this difficulty arose solely from the pre-assumption that the word was to be so continuously or monotonously spoken by a human being—I did not fail to perceive, in short, that the difficulty lay in the reconciliation of this monotony with the exercise of reason on the part of the creature repeating the word. Here, then, immediately arose the idea of a non-reasoning creature capable of speech; and, very naturally, a parrot, in the first instance, suggested itself, but was superseded forthwith by a Raven, as equally capable of speech, and infinitely more in keeping with the intended tone. I had now gone so far as the conception of a Raven—the bird of ill omen—monotonously repeating the one word, “Nevermore,” at the conclusion of each stanza, in a poem of melancholy tone, and in length about one hundred lines. Now, never losing sight of the object supremeness, or perfection, at all points, I asked myself—“Of all melancholy topics, what, according to the universal understanding of mankind, is the most melancholy?” Death—was the obvious reply.

items.prompt: What did the writer keep the same and what did he keep changing in the refrain?

tutor_only.confirm: The writer kept the sound's monotone and kept changing the thought.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The sentence beginning 'I resolved to diversify' says he would adhere to the monotone of sound while continually varying that of thought.
tutor_only.tell: He kept the sound of the refrain the same. He changed its thought each time.
help: The sentence about diversifying the effect says what he kept and what he varied.
He kept the sound; he varied the thought.
tutor_only.core_idea: The refrain keeps a steady sound while its thought changes.
accept_ideas: Keep the sound's monotone and change the thought.
Vary the thought while the refrain's sound stays steady.
The same sound with a new meaning each time.
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They say the writer kept the whole refrain exactly the same.
if_they_say.ask: Which sentence says the thought kept changing?

items.prompt: Why does the writer keep the refrain’s sound the same but change its thought?

tutor_only.confirm: To keep the repeated sound while making new effects by changing the thought.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The same sentence, 'I resolved to diversify... while I continually varied that of thought,' states both choices.
tutor_only.tell: He kept the sound so the refrain stayed familiar. He changed the thought so it stayed new.
help: Look at the sentence beginning 'I resolved to diversify.'
Find the two things he says he kept and varied.
tutor_only.core_idea: The writer repeats the refrain’s sound but varies its thought to create new effects.
accept_ideas: Keeping the sound the same while changing the thought creates new effects.
The repeated sound stays, but the meaning changes.
Varying the thought makes the refrain stronger.
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They say the writer changes both the sound and the thought.
if_they_say.ask: What does the sentence say stays the same?

if_they_say.when: They say the writer repeats the same thought.
if_they_say.ask: What does the writer say he keeps changing?

items.prompt: Why did the writer decide that one word was the best refrain?

tutor_only.confirm: The writer picked a one-word refrain because he planned to vary it often.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The sentence beginning 'Since its application was to be repeatedly varied' says the refrain must be brief so the variation stays easy.
tutor_only.tell: A brief refrain is easier to vary. A long sentence would be hard to vary often.
help: The sentence about repeated variation says why the refrain must be brief.
tutor_only.core_idea: A brief refrain fits frequent variation; a long one would be too hard to vary.
accept_ideas: A long refrain would be too hard to vary often.
The writer wanted a short refrain so he could change how it was used.
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: The student says the writer chose one word because it was sonorous.
if_they_say.ask: Which sentence links refrain length to frequent variation?

items.prompt: The writer chooses the word “Nevermore”—what does that choice do for the reader?

tutor_only.confirm: It has a sonorous sound and fits the poem’s melancholy tone.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The sentence beginning 'The sound of the refrain being thus determined' says he needed a word with that sound and in keeping with the melancholy tone; the next sentence says 'Nevermore' was the first word that presented itself.
tutor_only.tell: He needed a word with the right sound and the right tone. 'Nevermore' came first.
help: The sentence about fixing the sound says what the word had to match.
Find the word he says presented itself first.
tutor_only.core_idea: The writer chose “Nevermore” because its sound is sonorous and it keeps the melancholy tone.
accept_ideas: It has the long o and r sound.
not_required: Saying it was the first word
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: Says the word was chosen only because it came first.
if_they_say.ask: Which sentence says the word had to keep the poem’s melancholy tone?

items.prompt: After planning the refrain, what new problem does the writer work on next?

tutor_only.confirm: He needs a reason to keep using the word 'Nevermore.'
tutor_only.correct_reason: The first sentence of part 3 says 'The next desideratum was a pretext for the continuous use of the one word “Nevermore.”'
tutor_only.tell: He had the word and the refrain. Next he needed a reason to repeat 'Nevermore.'
help: Look at the first sentence of the last part.
tutor_only.core_idea: The writer shifts from planning how the refrain varies to finding a reason for its repeated word.
accept_ideas: He needs a reason for repeating 'Nevermore.'
He moves from planning the refrain to justifying the repeated word.
The plan changes to making the repetition believable.
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They say the writer changes the refrain to a parrot.
if_they_say.ask: Which sentence says he replaced the parrot with a Raven?
